name: source-foundation
title: Source Foundation
description: Elattar Design System foundation: the four canonical stylesheets (tokens, typeset, motion, utilities), the globals.css entry, the tailwind-merge config, the stylesheet-driven spring/duration reader, and the Icon/IconSwap primitives every component depends on.

/* ============================================================================
   TOKENS — the foundation, and the only place a value is chosen

   Faces, the dark variant, the brand ramps (`@theme static`), the shadcn
   semantic mapping (`@theme inline`), the light and dark theme blocks, and the
   `@layer base` document defaults.

   THIS FILE IS THE ONLY DECLARING CONTEXT. There is no `@theme` block and no
   bare `:root` / `.light` / `.dark` block anywhere else in the system — with
   one stated exception: motion.css carries a second `@theme static` holding the
   duration and easing scale, so time is defined beside the keyframes that
   spend it. Everything else reads these by `var()` or by a token utility.

   Imported by `app/globals.css`, which is the entry `components.json` names.
   ========================================================================= */

@font-face {
  font-family: "Inter Local";
  src: url("/fonts/inter-variable.woff2") format("woff2");
  font-style: normal;
  font-weight: 100 900;
  font-display: swap;
}

@custom-variant dark (&:is(.dark *));

/* ============================================================================
   ELATTAR'S DESIGN SYSTEM — BRAND TOKENS

   The palette itself: theme-independent, because a blue is a blue whichever
   surface it lands on. What changes between light and dark is which member of
   a ramp a given ROLE points at, and that lives in the theme blocks below.

   Two roles, and the whole colour story is in their names:
     `action`  the thing that acts — buttons, links, focus, selection, the agent
     `value`   the thing that is worth something — money, premium, reward, rarity

   They are named for what they mean rather than for what they look like, which
   is the difference between rebranding this system in five lines and rebranding
   it in seven hundred. This ramp has already been purple-and-gold, and it went
   to wine-and-amethyst and back; it is blue-and-lime today. No component knew
   or had to change on any of those moves — which is the claim this file exists
   to keep true.

   Balance target: ~70% neutral surfaces / ~20% action / ~10% value.
   ========================================================================= */
/* `static` is load-bearing, not a preference. Tailwind v4 tree-shakes @theme
   tokens that no utility class references — and the shadcn block below points at
   these by var(). A brand token used only by a derived alias would be shaken
   out, leaving e.g. `--accent` resolving to nothing. `static` emits them all. */
@theme static {
  /* Drop Tailwind's stock scales for the two hues we now occupy, so
     `text-blue-500` cannot resolve to an off-brand blue beside our own. Purple
     goes too: it was this system's action ramp two brands ago and a stock
     purple is the drift that would read as a survivor of it.
     Must precede our own keys. */
  --color-blue-*: initial;
  --color-lime-*: initial;
  --color-purple-*: initial;

  /* ── The two ramps — the ONLY colours outside shadcn's token set ──────────
     Three blues, three limes. Nothing else. Monochrome comes from zinc via the
     shadcn semantic tokens below.

     EACH RAMP HAS EXACTLY ONE TEXT-SAFE SHADE PER THEME, and it is not the same
     shade in both. `-bright` clears AA on the dark background; `-dark` clears it
     on the light one. Neither is safe on the other. That is why no component
     ever writes `text-action-bright` — it writes `text-action-ink`, which the
     theme blocks point at whichever end is legible here.
     `npm run dev` → /design-system/colors measures every one of them live, in
     whichever theme you are looking at.

     BLUE PUTS THE ACTION RAMP CLEAR OF EVERY STATE HUE, which is the thing the
     wine brand could not do: wine shared a hue family with `--destructive` and
     had to buy its separation with chroma and lightness. Here §1.5's clearance
     comes back for free — blue is 143° off amber, 158° off crimson, and the one
     hue it does sit near is `info`, which is why `info` is cyan rather than the
     blue 400 it started as. */
  /* The hexes are what these actually rasterise to, read off the live page.
     They were annotated #93C5FD / #2563EB / #1D4ED8 — Tailwind's blue 300 / 600
     / 700 — which is where the ramp was sampled from, but the `hsl()` values
     were never exactly those and the comment said otherwise for three brands. */
  --color-action-bright: hsl(213 94% 78%); /* #92C2FC · ink on dark   */
  --color-action: hsl(217 91% 53%); /* #1A6EF4 · the fill      */
  --color-action-dark: hsl(224 76% 33%); /* #143694 · ink on light  */

  --color-value-bright: #d9f99d; /* lime, lifted   */
  --color-value: #a3e635; /* lime, the fill */
  --color-value-dark: #4d7c0f; /* lime, ink on light */

  /* The ink that sits ON the value foil — and the one foreground in this system
     that deliberately does NOT flip with the theme.
     Everything else pairs a foreground to a surface that changes: text on
     `--background` inverts because the background inverts. The foil does not.
     It is an opaque metal ramp mixed from the three limes above, so it is the
     same lime on a white page as on a black one, and its label has to be dark
     in both.
     `text-background` was doing this job, which was correct in a dark-only
     system and became a contrast failure the moment light mode existed: on
     light, `--background` is white, so the premium button rendered white on
     lime.
     Measured against every stop of the foil by rasterising each one — the
     `color-mix(in oklab, …)` stops compute to `oklab()` and have to be painted
     to read honestly, not parsed. Lime is a high-luminance hue, so every stop
     clears AAA with room to spare; the live figures are printed on
     /design-system/colors. */
  --color-value-foreground: hsl(240 10% 8%);

  /* ── State ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     shadcn ships only --destructive, so these three are ours. Each is chosen to
     clear WCAG AA as text in BOTH themes — the colours page proves it by
     measuring them live rather than asserting it here.

     Two of the three sit where they do because of the action ramp, not in spite
     of it:

       `info` was blue 400. Once `action` became blue, an informational alert and
       the brand were the same colour, so a notice read as a promotion. It is
       cyan — still cool, still obviously "here is a fact", no longer the brand.

       `success` was green 400, which sat a few degrees from lime. A completed
       action and a valuable one must not be confusable when both appear in the
       same row, so success is a deeper emerald and the gap is open.

     `warning` has not moved through two rebrands and does not need to: amber is
     forty degrees off lime, which is §1.5's working clearance, and 143° off the
     action ramp. */
  --color-success: #10b981; /* emerald 500 */
  --color-warning: #fbbf24; /* amber 400   */
  --color-info: #22d3ee; /* cyan 400    */

  /* The deep end of each state hue.
     The three above were picked for near-black and are correct there. On white
     they are decorative, not legible: amber 400 measures about 1.7:1 and cyan
     400 about 1.9:1, so `text-warning` on a light surface was unreadable and
     nothing said so. The brand ramps solved this with `-ink`; the state colours
     never got the same treatment, which is the gap these close. */
  --color-success-deep: #047857; /* emerald 700 */
  --color-warning-deep: #b45309; /* amber 700   */
  --color-info-deep: #0e7490; /* cyan 700    */
  /* shadcn's `--destructive` is one red in both themes, and on near-black it
     measures about 3.1:1 — fine as a fill, too weak as a glyph or a label. This
     is its lifted counterpart, used only where destructive has to carry text. */
  --color-destructive-lifted: #f87171; /* red 400 */
  --color-destructive-deep: hsl(0 72.2% 46%); /* light-theme ink on red washes */

  /* ── Typography ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     TWO FACES, AND ONLY TWO. Inter owns words — body, headings, navigation,
     labels, the display step. Geist Mono owns code, identifiers and figures.

     There is no third. `--font-heading` was Inter written out a second time
     under another name, so a heading and a paragraph could silently disagree
     about their face; `--font-accent` was Redaction, a display serif carried
     for exactly one word on one page, and both it and the `.type-accent` role
     it served are gone.

     Inter is loaded by the `@font-face` at the top of this file rather than by
     `next/font/local` in `app/layout.tsx`, and that is a deliberate choice: the
     stylesheet is what a consumer installs, so a system whose sans face is
     wired up in an app's root layout arrives at that consumer without one.
     Geist Mono is the exception and has to be — `--font-geist-mono` is written
     onto <html> by the `geist` package at runtime. */
  --font-sans: "Inter Local", ui-sans-serif, system-ui, sans-serif;
  --font-mono: var(--font-geist-mono), ui-monospace, monospace;

  /* Tailwind's `font-*` utilities are part of the component vocabulary, so
     their values belong here too. Without these aliases, `font-medium` in a
     primitive follows the framework default rather than this type system. */
  --font-weight-normal: 400;
  --font-weight-medium: 500;
  --font-weight-semibold: 600;

  /* ── Tracking ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     NINE OF THE SEVENTEEN ROLES ARE TRACKED, and this comment used to say the
     contract specified none. Flutter 0.0.3 tightens everything at the top of
     the scale and everything set in mono: `display` -0.03, `h1` and
     `number-xl` -0.02, `h2` -0.015, and `h3`, `identifier` and the four
     smaller numerics -0.01. `h4`, `lead`, `body`, `small`, `nav`, `badge` and
     `code` stay `normal`. `styles/typeset.css` is where each role spends one
     of these; the mapping is asserted, role by role, in
     `test/foundation/typography-contract.test.ts`.

     `--tracking-snug` is new and exists for exactly one role, `h2`. It is not
     furniture: the contract asks for -0.015em there and a literal in
     `typeset.css` would be a hardcoded value in a file whose whole job is to
     stop those.

     `--tracking-num` is no longer unspent — it is the tightening the five
     numeric roles and `identifier` now take. The four that are gone — tag,
     badge, label, micro, running 0.12em to 0.18em — were the furniture
     ladder's wide-tracked uppercase steps, and they went with the roles that
     spent them. `--tracking-cta` stays because Button's `emphasis="caps"`
     variant is a component decision about one control, which is exactly where
     case and tracking now live. */
  --tracking-display: -0.03em;
  --tracking-tight: -0.02em;
  --tracking-snug: -0.015em;
  --tracking-num: -0.01em;
  --tracking-cta: 0.09em;

  /* ── Type sizes and line heights ─────────────────────────────────────────
     TWO TOKENS PER ROLE, holding that role's PHONE step. The tablet and
     desktop steps redefine these same names in the two media blocks below
     this `@theme`, so a role has exactly ONE owner for each of its values and
     both readers of that value move together.

     THE TWO READERS ARE WHY THE STEPS ARE TOKENS AND NOT LITERALS.
     `styles/typeset.css` used to write the tablet and desktop sizes itself as
     literal rem, on the reasoning that a token only one media block can read
     is a name with no second reader. That reasoning stopped holding once
     Flutter 0.0.3 made every role responsive. Tailwind v4 compiles
     `text-small` to `font-size: var(--text-small)` — verified in the built
     stylesheet, which is the only authority on what a class emits — so the
     utility and the `.type-*` class read the SAME custom property. Redefining
     the property under a media query moves both; writing literals in
     `typeset.css` would have moved only the class, and left every
     `text-sm` in the vendored shadcn components frozen at the phone step.

     THERE IS NOW A STEP BELOW 14px, and this comment used to say there was
     not. The old ladder's 10px-to-13px furniture roles were removed because
     each one existed to carry a colour or a case some component did not want,
     not because 12px is indefensible. Flutter 0.0.3 sets the shared contract:
     `body` starts at 14 on a phone and reaches 16 on a desktop, `small`
     starts at 12 and reaches 14, and `badge` starts at 10. A phone reads at a
     shorter distance than a laptop; the role keeps its meaning and grows with
     the viewport instead of holding one size everywhere. `test/foundation/
     typography-contract.test.ts` asserts all seventeen against
     `lib/ds/platform-contract.ts`, at all three widths.

     Sizes are `rem`, never `px`, so browser text zoom and a user's own root
     size keep working. The pixel comments are the contract's numbers at a
     16px root. */
  --text-display: 2.25rem; /* 36 */
  --text-h1: 1.875rem; /* 30 */
  --text-h2: 1.625rem; /* 26 */
  --text-h3: 1.25rem; /* 20 */
  --text-h4: 1.125rem; /* 18 */
  --text-lead: 1.125rem; /* 18 */
  --text-body: 0.875rem; /* 14 */
  --text-small: 0.75rem; /* 12 */
  --text-nav: 0.75rem; /* 12 */
  --text-badge: 0.625rem; /* 10 */
  --text-code: 0.75rem; /* 12 */
  --text-identifier: 0.75rem; /* 12 */
  --text-number-sm: 0.75rem; /* 12 */
  --text-number-base: 0.875rem; /* 14 */
  --text-number-md: 1.25rem; /* 20 */
  --text-number-lg: 1.875rem; /* 30 */
  --text-number-xl: 2.25rem; /* 36 */

  --leading-display: 2.5rem; /* 40 */
  --leading-h1: 2.25rem; /* 36 */
  --leading-h2: 2rem; /* 32 */
  --leading-h3: 1.75rem; /* 28 */
  --leading-h4: 1.5rem; /* 24 */
  --leading-lead: 1.75rem; /* 28 */
  --leading-body: 1.25rem; /* 20 */
  --leading-small: 1rem; /* 16 */
  --leading-nav: 1rem; /* 16 */
  --leading-badge: 0.875rem; /* 14 */
  --leading-code: 1.125rem; /* 18 */
  --leading-identifier: 1.125rem; /* 18 */
  --leading-number-sm: 1rem; /* 16 */
  --leading-number-base: 1.25rem; /* 20 */
  --leading-number-md: 1.75rem; /* 28 */
  --leading-number-lg: 2.25rem; /* 36 */
  --leading-number-xl: 2.5rem; /* 40 */

  /* Tailwind's own steps, repointed at ours.
     Without this the product runs TWO type scales side by side, and the sixty
     vendored shadcn components are written in `text-sm` / `text-xs`. Rewriting
     them all would fight the "one vocabulary, and it is shadcn's" rule, so the
     scale is aliased instead.

     These four now track the responsive roles they point at, which is the
     second thing the media blocks below bought. `text-sm` used to be frozen at
     the one size `--text-small` ever had; it is 12 / 13 / 14 now, the same
     three steps `.type-small` walks. The aliases are also finally honest about
     Tailwind's own intent — its `xs` means 12 and its `base` means 16, and at
     the ends of the range each one now lands there. */
  --text-xs: var(--text-small); /* 12 → 14 */
  --text-sm: var(--text-small); /* 12 → 14 */
  --text-base: var(--text-body); /* 14 → 16 */
  --text-lg: var(--text-lead); /* 18 → 20 */

  /* ── Radius ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     `xs` exists for tips and swatches only — a tooltip arrow, a chart legend
     key. Nothing with content in it should ever be this sharp. */
  /* ── Content width ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     The two measures the documentation shell is built on, and the only two
     widths in this system that are neither a component's size nor a fraction
     of the viewport. `shell` is the outer frame the sidebar and main column
     share; `content` is the reading column inside it, held to roughly 90
     characters at the body size so a paragraph never runs past a comfortable
     line. They were inline pixel values until the guard learned to look for
     them. */
  --width-shell: 1680px;
  --width-content: 1080px;
  /* The documentation stage's code view, capped so a page stays a reference.

     `PreviewCode` swaps source into the same frame the specimen occupies. An
     eighty-line specimen uncapped pushes every following section below the
     fold, and the reader scrolls through code they did not ask for to reach
     the next component. 28rem is roughly twenty-two lines at `--text-code`,
     which is enough to read a whole small specimen without scrolling and
     enough of a large one to see what shape it is. */
  --height-doc-code: 28rem;
  /* The Preview stage's floor. A component page opens on its specimen, and a
     stage that shrinks to a lone 36px button reads as an empty page; the
     owner's call is 640px so the opening frame is a real stage whatever is
     on it. Only the Preview section's stage — a state grid further down is
     sized by its content. */
  --height-doc-stage: 40rem;
  /* How much of the viewport a pinned documentation rail may occupy.

     Both rails are desktop-only by construction, so this is only ever applied
     to a desktop viewport. A rail that fits inside it never notices. It is the
     long ones — the component family lists, a component page's outline — that
     stop short of the fold instead of running the eye to the bottom edge of
     the screen, so the rail reads as a panel with room around it rather than a
     column of text poured into the window.

     The `min()` is the short-viewport case: below about 500px of height, 80dvh
     is MORE than what is left under the sticky header, and the rail's bottom
     would fall off the screen carrying its last few rows with it. The second
     term is what is actually available; whichever is smaller wins. */
  --height-doc-rail: min(80dvh, calc(100dvh - var(--height-site-header)));
  /* The site measure, and the reading measure inside it.

     `--width-page` is the cap for customer-facing pages — FAQ, about, contact,
     help, legal. `/design-system/spacing` has documented this number as prose
     since the grid section was written ("Product pages cap at 1320px") while no
     token existed, so a page container had nothing to read and `max-w-[1320px]`
     fails §0's guard. Written down here, it is one edit instead of a claim.

     `--width-prose` is narrower than `--width-content` on purpose and they are
     not interchangeable. 1080 is a documentation column carrying specimens,
     panels and tables beside the copy; 720 is a column carrying nothing but
     sentences, and a terms-of-service paragraph at 1080 loses its place on the
     return sweep. The number is a measured character count on the live page at
     `--text-body`, not a ratio — remeasure it if the body face or size moves. */
  --width-page: 1200px;
  --width-prose: 720px;
  /* The reading rail: a table of contents, an anchor list, an article's
     metadata column. 240px, the same measure the documentation sidebar
     already uses, and on the 8-point scale. It is not `--width-sidebar`:
     that one is the app shell's navigation panel and collapses to an icon
     rail, which a rail beside prose never does. */
  --width-rail: 15rem;
  /* The site header's own height, so an anchor can be scrolled clear of it.
     `scroll-padding-top` on `html` reads this (see @layer base), which is why
     it is a token rather than a number repeated in a sticky header, a sticky
     sidebar's `100dvh -` and a `scroll-mt-*` three files apart. It was all
     three of those before this line existed. */
  --height-site-header: 4rem;
  /* Where an anchored heading comes to rest: clear of the header, plus one
     32px step of air so the heading is not welded to the chrome above it.
     6rem = 96px, which is exactly the `scroll-mt-24` that `DsSection` used to
     hand-set — the same number, now derived from the header it was guessing
     at, and in one place instead of on every section element. */
  --scroll-offset: calc(var(--height-site-header) + var(--spacing) * 8);

  /* ── App-shell sidebar ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
     The three measures `ui/sidebar.tsx` is built on. They were module-level
     string constants inside that component — 16rem, 18rem and 3rem, written
     by hand — which is the one thing §0 does not allow, and which the guard
     never caught because a bare string in a `.tsx` file is not a class.

     All three land on the 8-point scale: 256, 288 and 48. The mobile measure
     is wider than the desktop one on purpose — a sheet has no rail beside it
     competing for the eye, so it can afford the extra 32px, and a touch
     target inside it wants the room. The icon measure is the collapsed rail:
     48px, which is the hit-target floor from §7, not a smaller number that
     happens to fit an icon. */
  --width-sidebar: 16rem;
  --width-sidebar-mobile: 18rem;
  --width-sidebar-icon: 3rem;

  /* ── The hit-target floor ───────────────────────────────────────────────
     44 CSS pixels, the minimum effective size of anything a finger can hit.

     The number was real and written down — RULES §7, and `TouchTargets.minimum`
     in the Flutter counterpart — but it was not a token, so a control declaring
     its own minimum had nothing to read. What that produces is `min-h-11`: the
     right measurement, on the 8-point scale, saying nothing about WHY it is
     eleven steps rather than ten. A named token is the difference between a
     number that happens to be correct and a number that is correct on purpose,
     and it is the one the next person raising the floor has to edit.

     It is a floor on the target, not on the drawing. A control may look smaller
     — a 20px checkbox, a nested dismiss ✕ — and reclaim the area with negative
     margin (§7); the default `Button` is a stated 40px exception, because it
     has to sit level with a 40px `Input`. */
  --size-target-min: 2.75rem; /* 44 */

  --radius-xs: 2px;
  --radius-sm: 6px;
  --radius-md: 10px;
  --radius-lg: 12px;
  --radius-xl: 16px;
  --radius-2xl: 20px;
  --radius-3xl: 24px;
  /* The soft-slab step. Not part of the container ladder's normal range — it
     exists for the one shape that is a *panel of content* rather than a box
     around it: a full-width metric slab on a narrow column, where 24px still
     reads as a rectangle with the corners taken off. 32px is on the 8-point
     scale and is the last step before a 180px-tall card starts reading as a
     lozenge. Do not reach for it on anything that sits in a grid with `lg`
     cards; two radii on one screen is a drift, not a hierarchy. */
  --radius-4xl: 32px;
  --radius-pill: 999px;

  /* ── Elevation ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     Two families. e1–e4 are ambient depth. The rest are MACHINE surfaces:
     things that look like they can be physically pressed. That is why a
     button here has an inner top highlight and an inner bottom shade rather
     than a flat fill.

     THE GEOMETRY IS FIXED; THE INK IS NOT. Every colour below is a `--ink-*` or
     `--rim` variable that the theme blocks set, because a shadow that works on
     near-black is wrong on white twice over: pure black at 60% on a light
     surface reads as dirt rather than depth, and the inner top highlight that
     makes a dark button look lit does nothing at all against white. Light mode
     gets weaker, cooler, tighter ink and an inverted rim — same shapes, same
     names, same components. */
  --shadow-e1: 0 1px 1px var(--ink-2), 0 1px 3px var(--ink-1);
  --shadow-e2: 0 1px 2px var(--ink-2), 0 4px 10px -2px var(--ink-2);
  --shadow-e3: 0 2px 4px var(--ink-2), 0 14px 28px -8px var(--ink-3);
  --shadow-e4: 0 4px 8px var(--ink-3), 0 28px 56px -14px var(--ink-4);

  /* Raised key with a side wall — travels down into its socket when pressed. */
  --shadow-key: 0 4px 0 var(--wall), 0 7px 12px var(--ink-3);
  --shadow-key-down: 0 1px 0 var(--wall), inset 0 2px 5px var(--ink-3);
  /* Sunken socket. Inputs sit in one of these. */
  --shadow-pressed: inset 0 2px 5px var(--ink-3), inset 0 1px 2px var(--ink-4);

  /* Control depth. btn-primary carries the action cast. */
  --shadow-btn:
    inset 0 1px 0 var(--rim), inset 0 -2px 4px var(--ink-2), 0 1px 2px var(--ink-2),
    0 3px 8px -2px var(--ink-2);
  --shadow-btn-primary:
    inset 0 1px 0 var(--rim-strong), inset 0 -2px 5px var(--ink-2),
    0 1px 2px var(--ink-2),
    0 4px 10px -2px color-mix(in oklab, var(--color-action) 55%, transparent);
  --shadow-btn-value:
    inset 0 1px 0 var(--rim-strong), inset 0 -2px 5px var(--ink-1),
    0 1px 2px var(--ink-2),
    0 4px 10px -2px color-mix(in oklab, var(--color-value) 45%, transparent);
  --shadow-btn-down: inset 0 2px 4px var(--ink-3), 0 1px 1px var(--ink-1);
  --shadow-chip:
    inset 0 1px 0 var(--rim), inset 0 -1px 2px var(--ink-2), 0 1px 2px var(--ink-2);

  /* Rationed glows — selection and reward only. */
  --shadow-glow-action:
    0 0 0 1px color-mix(in oklab, var(--color-action-bright) 45%, transparent),
    0 10px 34px -8px color-mix(in oklab, var(--color-action) 60%, transparent);
  --shadow-glow-value:
    0 0 0 1px color-mix(in oklab, var(--color-value) 45%, transparent),
    0 10px 34px -8px color-mix(in oklab, var(--color-value) 42%, transparent);
}

/* ============================================================================
   TYPE SCALE — THE TABLET AND DESKTOP STEPS

   The `@theme static` block above holds every role's PHONE step. These two
   blocks redefine the same custom properties at the two breakpoints, which is
   the whole responsive mechanism: `.type-body` and `text-base` and
   `leading-body` all compile to `var(--text-body)` / `var(--leading-body)`, so
   moving the property moves every reader at once and none of them can drift.

   PLAIN `:root`, NOT `@theme`. Tailwind's `@theme` may only appear at the top
   level — it is a compile-time declaration, not a cascade participant — so the
   steps are written as ordinary custom-property declarations. They win on
   source order at equal specificity, which is why these blocks sit after the
   `@theme static` block and not before it.

   TWO BREAKPOINTS, and there is no third. Phone is below 768, tablet is 768
   through 1023, desktop is 1024 and up — the same three bands Flutter 0.0.3
   uses, and the same two `(width >= …)` queries `styles/typeset.css` has
   always used. No `clamp()`: fluid type cannot be asserted at a value, only at

/* ============================================================================
   SHADCN SEMANTIC MAPPING
   Every base component reads these. Remapping them here is what makes stock
   shadcn look like this system without patching each component.
   ========================================================================= */
@theme inline {
  --color-background: var(--background);
  --color-foreground: var(--foreground);
  --color-card: var(--card);
  --color-card-foreground: var(--card-foreground);
  --color-popover: var(--popover);
  --color-popover-foreground: var(--popover-foreground);
  --color-primary: var(--primary);
  --color-primary-foreground: var(--primary-foreground);
  --color-secondary: var(--secondary);
  --color-secondary-foreground: var(--secondary-foreground);
  --color-muted: var(--muted);
  --color-muted-foreground: var(--muted-foreground);
  --color-accent: var(--accent);
  --color-accent-foreground: var(--accent-foreground);
  --color-destructive: var(--destructive);
  --color-destructive-foreground: var(--destructive-foreground);
  --color-border: var(--border);
  --color-input: var(--input);
  --color-ring: var(--ring);
  --color-chart-1: var(--chart-1);
  --color-chart-2: var(--chart-2);
  --color-chart-3: var(--chart-3);
  --color-chart-4: var(--chart-4);
  --color-chart-5: var(--chart-5);
  --color-sidebar: var(--sidebar);
  --color-sidebar-foreground: var(--sidebar-foreground);
  --color-sidebar-primary: var(--sidebar-primary);
  --color-sidebar-primary-foreground: var(--sidebar-primary-foreground);
  --color-sidebar-accent: var(--sidebar-accent);
  --color-sidebar-accent-foreground: var(--sidebar-accent-foreground);
  --color-sidebar-border: var(--sidebar-border);
  --color-sidebar-ring: var(--sidebar-ring);

  /* The agent family. Three tokens, so `bg-agent/8`, `text-agent` and
     `bg-agent-muted` are utilities like any other rather than inline colour. */
  --color-agent: var(--agent);
  --color-agent-muted: var(--agent-muted);
  --color-scrim: var(--scrim);

  /* The text-safe end of each brand ramp, resolved per theme.

     This is the token a glyph names. `--color-action-bright` is legible on
     near-black and illegible on white; `--color-action-dark` is the reverse. A
     component cannot know which surface it is on, so it does not choose — it
     writes `text-action-ink` and the theme block answers.

     This is the one piece of the colour system with no shadcn equivalent and no
     dark-only shortcut, and it is what made light mode possible without editing
     a single component. */
  --color-action-ink: var(--action-ink);
  --color-value-ink: var(--value-ink);
  /* Same contract for the three state hues: the token a glyph or a label names,
     resolved to whichever end is legible in this theme. */
  --color-success-ink: var(--success-ink);
  --color-warning-ink: var(--warning-ink);
  --color-info-ink: var(--info-ink);
  --color-destructive-ink: var(--destructive-ink);

  /* The tinted chat bubble's surface, and what it becomes when the bubble is
     itself a button or a link.

     It is a token rather than an inline `oklch(from …)` for the reason §1.7
     gives: it needed a `dark:` twin, and a colour that needs a `dark:` variant
     is a token that has not been written yet. The lightness stops differ per
     theme — a 0.93 wash is a pale blue on white and a glare on zinc 950 — so
     the theme block answers and the component never asks. */
  --color-bubble-tinted: var(--bubble-tinted);
  --color-bubble-tinted-hover: var(--bubble-tinted-hover);
}

/* ============================================================================
   SHADCN SEMANTIC TOKENS — THE ONE VOCABULARY
   There is a single naming system in this project and it is shadcn's. The page
   is `--background`, a container is `--card`, an overlay or fill is
   `--popover`, a hover surface is `--accent`, text is `--foreground` and
   `--muted-foreground`, hairlines are `--border`. These hold the literal
   values; nothing restates them under a second name.

   Brand tokens exist ONLY where shadcn has no equivalent — the action and value
   ramps, the rarity ladder, semantic states, the tints, `--color-sunken`,
   `--color-border-mid` / `-strong`, and the
   on-accent foregrounds. Each of those is named for its role, never numbered.
   ========================================================================= */
/* ── LIGHT ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   `:root` is light because that is what an unstyled document is, and because
   next-themes adds `.dark` rather than removing a class. `.light` is listed
   alongside it so an explicit light island inside a dark page — a printable
   panel, an embedded preview — resolves the same way.

   Light is not dark with the numbers flipped. Three things genuinely change
   rather than invert:

     Ink gets weaker and cooler. Pure black at 60% over white reads as grime;
     the same depth on paper comes from a slate-tinted shadow at a fifth of the
     opacity, spread tighter.

     The rim inverts its job. On dark, the inner top highlight is white and it
     is what makes a button look lit from above. On light there is no light to
     add, so the rim becomes near-white at high alpha purely to keep the top
     edge from muddying, and the bottom inner shade does the shaping instead.

     The ramps swap which end is text. `--action-ink` is the bright blue on
     dark and the deep blue on light; nothing that renders a glyph ever names
     an end of the ramp directly.
   ------------------------------------------------------------------------ */
:root,
.light {
  /* ── Monochrome: zinc, read upward ─────────────────────────────────────── */
  --background: hsl(0 0% 100%);
  --foreground: hsl(240 10% 3.9%);

  --card: hsl(0 0% 100%);
  --card-foreground: hsl(240 10% 3.9%);
  --popover: hsl(0 0% 100%);
  --popover-foreground: hsl(240 10% 3.9%);

  --secondary: hsl(240 4.8% 95.9%); /* zinc 100 */
  --secondary-foreground: hsl(240 5.9% 10%);
  --muted: hsl(240 4.8% 95.9%);
  /* Muted text is the one place light mode cannot mirror dark. On dark,
     --muted-foreground is zinc 300 at 12:1; the mirror image would be zinc 400
     on white, which measures 3.1:1 and fails.
     It is NOT zinc 500 either, which is what this line held for most of this
     system's life: zinc 500 cleared AA on `--background` at 4.83:1 and MISSED
     it on `--muted` at 4.40:1 — and `--muted-foreground` on `--muted` is the
     most repeated foreground/surface pair in the whole file. The failure was
     found during the wine brand and it is not a wine problem, so the deeper
     step carries back. Both pairs measured live on /design-system/colors. */
  --muted-foreground: hsl(240 4% 40%);
  --accent: hsl(240 4.8% 95.9%);
  --accent-foreground: hsl(240 5.9% 10%);

  --border: hsl(240 5.9% 90%);
  --input: hsl(240 5.9% 90%);

  /* The page's light source. See the `body` rule in @layer base. On paper the
     raise is almost nothing — a cool centre on a white page — because a visible
     gradient on white reads as a stain rather than as light. */
  --page-glow: hsl(240 30% 98%);

  /* ── Brand ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
  --primary: var(--color-action);
  --primary-foreground: hsl(0 0% 100%);
  --ring: var(--color-action);

  /* The text-safe end of each ramp, for this theme. Nothing writes
     `text-action-bright` — it writes `text-action-ink`, and this is where the
     answer differs between the two modes. */
  --action-ink: var(--color-action-dark);
  --value-ink: var(--color-value-dark);
  --success-ink: var(--color-success-deep);
  --warning-ink: var(--color-warning-deep);
  --info-ink: var(--color-info-deep);
  --destructive-ink: var(--color-destructive-deep);

  --destructive: hsl(0 72.2% 50.6%);
  --destructive-foreground: hsl(0 0% 98%);

  /* The tinted bubble, derived from the action ramp so it follows a rebrand.
     On white the tint has to be a pale wash: high lightness, chroma cut to
     40% so it reads as tinted paper rather than as a second brand colour. */
  --bubble-tinted: oklch(from var(--primary) 0.93 calc(c * 0.4) h);
  --bubble-tinted-hover: oklch(from var(--primary) 0.88 calc(c * 0.5) h);

  --radius: 10px;

  /* ── Shadow ink ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     Slate rather than black, and roughly a fifth of dark mode's opacity. The
     geometry in @theme static does not change; only what colour fills it. */
  --ink-1: hsl(240 20% 20% / 0.04);
  --ink-2: hsl(240 20% 20% / 0.07);
  --ink-3: hsl(240 20% 20% / 0.11);
  --ink-4: hsl(240 20% 20% / 0.16);
  --rim: hsl(0 0% 100% / 0.85);
  --rim-strong: hsl(0 0% 100% / 0.4);
  --wall: hsl(240 6% 82%);

  /* The same rule as `-ink`, mirrored: on paper the LEGIBLE end of every ramp
     is the deep one. `--color-action-bright` sat at `--chart-3` here for most of
     this system's life and measured 1.81:1 on white — a chart line you cannot
     see. That is a legibility bug rather than a brand choice, so this ordering
     survives the return to blue and lime. §1.3 already sanctions a raw state hue
     as a chart mark: the shape carries the meaning, not the colour. */
  --chart-1: var(--color-action);
  --chart-2: var(--color-value-dark);
  --chart-3: var(--color-info-deep);
  --chart-4: var(--color-action-dark);
  --chart-5: var(--color-success-deep);

  /* ── Sidebar ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     Eight tokens that all resolve to something else.

     This was the last stock shadcn left in the file — literal zinc, written
     out by hand, sitting between two blocks that had both been reasoned
     about. It survived because nothing imported `ui/sidebar.tsx`, so nobody
     ever saw it in either theme.

     Every value already existed under a name that means something, and the
     roles come from the sidebar this system already ships (`DsSidebar`): a
     resting nav item is `--muted-foreground`, hovering or activating it takes
     it to `--foreground`, and a hairline separates it from the page rather
     than a fill. Six of the eight were numerically identical to the token
     that now names them; only the surface and the resting text actually move.

     The block is repeated verbatim in the dark theme on purpose. It could be
     declared once here — every referent already answers per theme, so
     substitution would do the rest — but that only holds while `.dark` sits
     on the same element as `:root`. The moment a SUBTREE is themed, which is
     exactly what a side-by-side light/dark specimen does, a `:root`-only
     declaration would inherit the wrong theme's surface into it. */
  --sidebar: var(--card);
  --sidebar-foreground: var(--muted-foreground);
  --sidebar-primary: var(--primary);
  --sidebar-primary-foreground: var(--primary-foreground);
  --sidebar-accent: var(--accent);
  --sidebar-accent-foreground: var(--accent-foreground);
  --sidebar-border: var(--border);
  --sidebar-ring: var(--ring);

  /* ── Agent ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
  /* `-dark`, not the fill — the same answer `--action-ink` gives on this theme,
     and for the same reason.

     §1.3 is absolute: only the text-safe end of a ramp may carry a glyph. The
     dark block obeys it and says so in a comment (`--agent` resolves to the
     lifted end because it is read as a foreground far more often than as a
     fill: eleven `text-agent` uses against two marks about a pixel and a half
     across). This line did NOT obey it, and pointed at the fill — the one shade
     §1.3 names as never text — for the whole life of the light theme.

     Measured rather than reasoned: with the fill here, a `text-agent` link
     inside the user's own bubble rasterised at **4.25:1** on `--agent-muted`,
     and the slash palette's active row at **4.17:1** on `--accent`. Both under
     4.5. On `--color-action-dark` they are **9.80** and **9.62**. The two marks that
     use it as a fill — the streaming caret and the active-conversation dot —
     only get more visible on paper for the change. */
  --agent: var(--color-action-dark);
  --agent-muted: hsl(213 100% 97%);
  --scrim: hsl(240 10% 3.9% / 0.28);
  /* ── Media scrim ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     The readability ramp over a photograph or a video, so a title placed
     directly on media stays legible without an opaque card under it. The web
     half of Flutter's `media-scrim`, and the one capability the convergence
     audit found with no implementation at all — `--scrim` above is a flat
     panel dim behind a drawer, which is a different thing wearing a similar
     name.

     THEME-INDEPENDENT ON PURPOSE. Media does not change when the application
     flips theme, so the ink over it must not either: these four are declared
     once, here, and there is no dark-mode redefinition. The ink is black and
     the foreground is white regardless of `.dark`, because the thing being
     contrasted against is a photograph.

     The numbers are Flutter's `MediaScrimTokens`, copied rather than tuned:
     transparent through the upper half, a restrained bridge at 58%, and enough
     at the bottom edge for white title copy without becoming a slab. */
  --media-ink: hsl(0 0% 0%);
  --media-foreground: hsl(0 0% 100%);
  --media-scrim-mid-stop: 58%;
  --media-scrim-mid: 18%;
  --media-scrim-end: 82%;

  /* ── Bloom neutrals ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     The two values that make the cosmic bloom a different painting in each
     theme, and the reason it looked like grey smoke here until now.

     A blend mode has an IDENTITY — the colour that changes nothing. For
     `screen` that is black; for `multiply` it is white. The bloom's gradients
     fade out to `--bloom-void`, so on dark they fade to black and vanish under
     screen, and on light they fade to white and vanish under multiply. Fading
     to black on a white card, which is what they used to do, paints actual grey
     across the surface: not a dim bloom, a dirty one.

     `--bloom-hot` is the opposite end — the hottest point of the core, derived
     in the utility rather than declared here. On dark "hot" means lifted toward
     white. On light there is no light to add, so hot means the most PIGMENT:
     the core stays fully chromatic and the falloff does the fading. */
  --bloom-void: white;

  /* HOW MUCH PIGMENT THE BLOOM CARRIES, as multipliers rather than colours.

     This is the fix for a light-mode bloom that read as a weak wash no matter
     how far the opacity was pushed. `--bloom-1` and `--bloom-2` are the LIFTED
     ends of their ramps — `--color-action-bright` is a pale blue — which is
     correct on dark, where hot means lifted toward white. Multiply that pale
     blue over a white card and almost nothing happens: multiply darkens BY the
     colour, so a colour that is already near-white cannot darken anything. The
     opacity was never the lever; the hue was.

     So light mode takes each bloom hue down in lightness and up in chroma
     before it reaches a gradient stop. Same hue, far more pigment.

     They are multipliers and not two more colour tokens on purpose: the five
     toast types and every Alert variant each set their own `--bloom-1` /
     `--bloom-2`, so a fixed pair here would have to be repeated per type and
     would fall out of step the first time one changed. */
  --bloom-l: 0.6; /* lightness  x */
  --bloom-c: 1.55; /* chroma     x */
  /* The core's hottest point. On paper there is no light to add, so hot simply
     means the most saturated the hue gets — no raise at all. */
  --bloom-lift: 0;
  --bloom-hot-c: 1;
  /* The halo under each sparkle, and the whole reason white stars work on a
     white panel. A bare white star on paper is invisible; the same star with a
     coloured bloom under it reads as a point of light with air around it.
     Chromatic on light, because the glow has to do the separating that the
     surface cannot.

     This replaced `--star-ink`, which was declared in both themes and read by
     nothing — an SVG data URI cannot resolve a CSS variable, so it could never
     have driven the fill it was named for. */
  --star-glow: color-mix(in oklab, var(--bloom-2) 85%, transparent);
  --star-glow-size: 3px;

  /* The avatar is the one part of the system that cannot be re-derived from
     the semantic tokens: the handoff draws these cubes for paper, and the dark
     set is already an inversion of that original. This is the original. */
  --agent-cube-top: hsl(240 20% 99%);
  --agent-cube-left: hsl(240 15% 94%);
  --agent-cube-right: hsl(240 14% 90%);
  --agent-cube-stroke: hsl(240 10% 79%);
  --agent-cube-accent: var(--color-action);
  --agent-cube-error-top: hsl(0 70% 88%);
  --agent-cube-error-left: hsl(0 65% 82%);
  --agent-cube-error-right: hsl(0 60% 75%);
  --agent-cube-error-stroke: hsl(0 55% 69%);
  --agent-cube-back: hsl(240 14% 86%);
  --agent-cube-ghost-ink: hsl(240 5% 54%);
  --agent-cube-accent-shade: hsl(217 45% 72%);

  /* ── Code highlighting ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
     `CodeBlock` (`parts/code-block.tsx`) used to paint every fence with
     `vscDarkPlus`, a theme object with its own baked-in colours — legible on
     the near-black surface `vscDarkPlus` was drawn for, and never re-read for
     light mode, which is why a code block stayed dark inside a paper page.
     These eight read the same `-ink`-grade tokens every other coloured glyph
     in the system does (§1.3), so the fence follows the theme instead of
     carrying one. Each is measured against `--muted` — the fence's own
     surface (`code-block.tsx` wraps `SyntaxHighlighter` in `bg-muted`) — in
     both themes; the ratios are recorded in the commits that added this
     block (the original six, then `--code-type`/`--code-variable` in fix
     round 1) and on `/design-system/components/code-block`.

     `--code-type` and `--code-variable` are the two added in fix round 1,
     when review found the first six covered only 6 of the ~27 Prism token
     classes the ten registered grammars actually emit — everything else
     (`class-name`, `tag`, `property`, `regex`, `boolean`…) fell back to
     plain `--foreground`, so real JS/TS/JSX/CSS rendered mostly monochrome.
     Rather than inventing 21 new tokens for 21 new Prism classes, each was
     grouped onto whichever of these eight roles it reads closest to —
     `code-block.tsx`'s `STYLED_PRISM_TOKEN_CLASSES` and
     `styles/utilities.css`'s `code-highlight` both list the full grouping;
     this file only had two roles missing entirely: a name for a KIND of
     thing (a class, a built-in, a tag, a CSS selector) and a name for a
     SPECIFIC thing (a property, a parameter, a variable, an attribute
     name). The two unused `-ink` tokens were sitting right there. */
  --code-keyword: var(--action-ink); /* control flow: if, return, const, @media, decorators */
  --code-string: var(--success-ink); /* quoted literals, URLs, CDATA        */
  --code-comment: var(--muted-foreground); /* already tuned as body text    */
  --code-function: var(--info-ink); /* calls and declarations               */
  --code-number: var(--value-ink); /* numeric/boolean/constant literals, regex */
  --code-punctuation: var(--foreground); /* structural marks, operators     */
  --code-type: var(--warning-ink); /* class-name, builtin, tag, CSS selector */
  --code-variable: var(--destructive-ink); /* property, parameter, variable, attr-name */
}

/* ── The voice orb's obsidian ──────────────────────────────────────────────
   A dark glass sphere. It is an object rather than a surface, so it is the
   same in both themes; only its reflection is tinted by --agent. */
:root {
  --orb-light: hsl(210 25% 97%);
  --orb-sheen: hsl(216 12% 64%);
  --orb-body: hsl(222 14% 23%);
  --orb-deep: hsl(228 22% 6%);
  --orb-glint: hsl(210 30% 88% / 0.5);
  --orb-flow: hsl(214 20% 82% / 0.32);
}

/* ── Shiki's CSS-variables theme, on the code roles ──────────────────────
   lib/code-theme.ts highlights every Shiki code block (AI Elements'
   CodeBlock, the fences inside a Streamdown reply) with Shiki's
   CSS-variables theme, which colours a token `var(--shiki-token-keyword)`
   rather than baking in a palette. These aliases put those names on the
   same eight `--code-*` roles the Prism highlighter uses, so code reads the
   same everywhere and follows the theme: declared on `:root`, which carries
   the theme class, so each alias resolves that theme's role. The ANSI names
   match the terminal's own mapping (`terminal-colors`, styles/utilities.css). */
:root {
  --shiki-foreground: var(--foreground);
  --shiki-background: transparent;
  --shiki-token-keyword: var(--code-keyword);
  --shiki-token-string: var(--code-string);
  --shiki-token-string-expression: var(--code-string);
  --shiki-token-link: var(--code-string);
  --shiki-token-comment: var(--code-comment);
  --shiki-token-function: var(--code-function);
  --shiki-token-constant: var(--code-number);
  --shiki-token-punctuation: var(--code-punctuation);
  --shiki-token-parameter: var(--code-variable);
  --shiki-token-inserted: var(--success-ink);
  --shiki-token-deleted: var(--destructive-ink);
  --shiki-token-changed: var(--warning-ink);
  --shiki-ansi-black: var(--muted-foreground);
  --shiki-ansi-bright-black: var(--muted-foreground);
  --shiki-ansi-red: var(--destructive-ink);
  --shiki-ansi-bright-red: var(--destructive-ink);
  --shiki-ansi-green: var(--success-ink);
  --shiki-ansi-bright-green: var(--success-ink);
  --shiki-ansi-yellow: var(--warning-ink);
  --shiki-ansi-bright-yellow: var(--warning-ink);
  --shiki-ansi-blue: var(--action-ink);
  --shiki-ansi-bright-blue: var(--action-ink);
  --shiki-ansi-magenta: var(--value-ink);
  --shiki-ansi-bright-magenta: var(--value-ink);
  --shiki-ansi-cyan: var(--info-ink);
  --shiki-ansi-bright-cyan: var(--info-ink);
  --shiki-ansi-white: var(--foreground);
  --shiki-ansi-bright-white: var(--foreground);
}

/* ── DARK ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   The mode this system was designed in, and still its default. Seventy per
   cent neutral, twenty action, ten value.
   ------------------------------------------------------------------------ */
.dark {
  /* ── Monochrome: zinc ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     Four dark steps and four light steps, mapped onto shadcn's semantic
     tokens. There is no parallel naming system — the page is --background, a
     container is --card, a fill is --muted, text is --foreground. */
  --background: hsl(240 10% 3.9%); /* zinc 950 */
  --foreground: hsl(0 0% 98%); /* zinc 50  */

  --card: hsl(240 5.9% 10%); /* zinc 900 */
  --card-foreground: hsl(0 0% 98%);
  --popover: hsl(240 5.9% 10%);
  --popover-foreground: hsl(0 0% 98%);

  --secondary: hsl(240 3.7% 15.9%); /* zinc 800 */
  --secondary-foreground: hsl(0 0% 98%);
  --muted: hsl(240 3.7% 15.9%);
  --muted-foreground: hsl(240 4.9% 83.9%); /* zinc 300 */
  --accent: hsl(240 5.3% 26.1%); /* zinc 700 */
  --accent-foreground: hsl(0 0% 98%);

  --border: hsl(240 3.7% 15.9%);
  --input: hsl(240 5.3% 26.1%);

  /* The page's light source. See the `body` rule in @layer base. A wide,
     off-centre raise two steps up the neutral from `--background`, so a zinc-950
     page reads as a deep room rather than as flat black paint. The falloff
     reveals `--background` itself, which is why the vignette can never go
     muddy — it is the absence of the glow, not a second gradient. */
  --page-glow: hsl(240 8% 10%);

  /* ── Brand ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
  --primary: var(--color-action);
  /* Pure white, not zinc 50 — the one value in this block that is NOT what it
     was before the wine brand. Zinc 50 on the action fill rasterises at
     **4.39:1**, which misses AA by 0.11 on the most-used control in the system,
     and it missed it for the whole life of the blue brand because nothing
     measured it. Pure white is 4.58:1. Light mode was already pure white here;
     this is the two themes agreeing rather than a new idea. */
  --primary-foreground: hsl(0 0% 100%);
  --ring: var(--color-action-bright);

  /* The text-safe end of each ramp, for this theme. On near-black that is the
     lifted end of both ramps: the fills measure ~3:1 and cannot carry a glyph. */
  --action-ink: var(--color-action-bright);
  /* `-bright`, not the mid — which is what §1.3's table says, and this line did
     not obey it for most of this system's life.
     It pointed at `--color-value` for as long as the value ramp was lime and got
     away with it: lime 400 has a luminance around 0.66, so even the mid shade
     cleared 10:1 on every dark surface. A darker value hue at the same lightness
     step carries a fraction of that luminance, and the same line rasterised at
     **4.13:1** on a dropdown row — measured on the live Navigation and Selection
     specimens, on the money figures those pages exist to show.
     Lime makes the mid safe again, and it is still not what the rule says. This
     stays on `-bright`: the point of the table is that the theme block answers
     with the end that is safe on ANY value ramp, so the next rebrand cannot
     reintroduce a failure nothing can catch. `check:tokens` has no opinion about
     which end of a ramp a theme block points at. */
  --value-ink: var(--color-value-bright);
  --success-ink: var(--color-success);
  --warning-ink: var(--color-warning);
  --info-ink: var(--color-info);
  --destructive-ink: var(--color-destructive-lifted);

  /* shadcn's own error token — the one non-monochrome state colour it ships */
  --destructive: hsl(0 72.2% 50.6%);
  --destructive-foreground: hsl(0 0% 98%);

  /* The same tint, inverted. On zinc 950 a wash has to be a deep one — the
     light stops would be a glare — so lightness drops and chroma stays cut.
     The component names one class for both; this is where they differ. */
  --bubble-tinted: oklch(from var(--primary) 0.3 calc(c * 0.4) h);
  --bubble-tinted-hover: oklch(from var(--primary) 0.35 calc(c * 0.5) h);

  --radius: 10px;

  /* ── Shadow ink ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     Black, and heavy. On a zinc-950 page a shadow has to be darker than the
     surface it falls on or it is invisible, which is why these run three to
     four times light mode's opacity. */
  --ink-1: rgb(0 0 0 / 0.35);
  --ink-2: rgb(0 0 0 / 0.5);
  --ink-3: rgb(0 0 0 / 0.6);
  --ink-4: rgb(0 0 0 / 0.75);
  --rim: rgb(255 255 255 / 0.14);
  --rim-strong: rgb(255 255 255 / 0.28);
  --wall: hsl(240 6% 8%);

  /* Charts read action → value, matching the accent story — but every member
     has to be a LEGIBLE MARK first, and that is what decides the ordering.
     A chart line is a 2px stroke with no foreground of its own, so §1.3's rule
     about marks applies to it exactly as it does to a progress fill. The
     original ordering ran down each ramp — action, action-bright, action-dark,
     value, value-dark — and put two deep shades on a zinc-900 card where they
     could not be seen; `--color-action-dark` is the worst of them. It survived
     because only one member failed outright under blue and lime, and three did
     once the brand went darker, which is when it was finally measured.
     So each token names the end of its ramp that reads HERE — the same answer
     `-ink` gives — and the two state hues that clear it fill the tail rather
     than a third unreadable deep shade. §1.3 already sanctions a raw state hue
     as a chart mark: the shape carries the meaning, not the colour.
     Every member is measured live against `--card` on /design-system/colors. */
  --chart-1: var(--color-action-bright);
  --chart-2: var(--color-value);
  --chart-3: var(--color-info);
  --chart-4: var(--color-value-bright);
  --chart-5: var(--color-success);

  /* The same eight as the light block, and identical by design — see the note
     there for why they are repeated rather than declared once in `:root`.

     Dark had drifted less than light. Seven of these were already numerically
     what the token now naming them resolves to, including the two that DO
     move on light: `--sidebar` was `--card` written out as zinc 900, and
     `--sidebar-foreground` was `--muted-foreground` written out as zinc 300.

     One value genuinely changes here. `--sidebar-accent` was zinc 800 — the
     `--muted` / `--secondary` step — and is now `--accent`, zinc 700. That is
     a deliberate correction rather than a side effect: §1.1 gives `--accent`
     one job, which is a hover surface, and hovering a nav item is what this
     token is for. It lifts the hover one step, which is the direction it
     should have gone in a theme this dark. */
  --sidebar: var(--card);
  --sidebar-foreground: var(--muted-foreground);
  --sidebar-primary: var(--primary);
  --sidebar-primary-foreground: var(--primary-foreground);
  --sidebar-accent: var(--accent);
  --sidebar-accent-foreground: var(--accent-foreground);
  --sidebar-border: var(--border);
  --sidebar-ring: var(--ring);

  /* ── Agent ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     The agent acts, so the agent is the action colour (§0) — value would have
     read as a paid feature and competed with the wallet.

     `--agent` resolves to the ramp's lifted end rather than the fill, because
     it is read as a foreground far more often than as one: eleven `text-agent`
     uses — links, tool glyphs, the slash prefix, the listening mic — against
     two solid marks, the streaming caret and the active-conversation dot, each
     about a pixel and a half across. §1's rule is absolute for the first group
     and harmless for the second, so there is one token rather than two. */
  --agent: var(--color-action-bright);
  /* Screen's identity is black, so the bloom fades to black and disappears.
     See the light block for why this is the one value that could not simply be
     shared between the two themes. */
  --bloom-void: black;
  /* Untouched. On near-black the ramp's lifted end is already exactly right —
     screen adds light, and the hue arrives as hot as it needs to be. */
  --bloom-l: 1;
  --bloom-c: 1;
  /* Hot means lifted almost to white, and desaturating as it goes, which is
     what makes the core read as a light source rather than as a bright patch
     of paint. */
  --bloom-lift: 0.85;
  --bloom-hot-c: 0.5;
  /* On glass the star is already the brightest thing in its corner, so the
     halo only has to soften the edge — white, and half the spread. */
  --star-glow: rgb(255 255 255 / 0.5);
  --star-glow-size: 2px;
  /* The agent's own turn in the transcript. One step off --card toward the
     action hue: enough that whose turn it is survives a squint, not so much
     that a long answer becomes a coloured slab. The user's turn stays on
     --card. */
  --agent-muted: hsl(217 40% 13%);
  /* The dim a panel drops over the console it belongs to — --background, held
     back enough that the transcript stays legible underneath it. */
  --scrim: hsl(240 10% 3.9% / 0.66);

  /* ── Agent avatar: the isometric cube scene ─────────────────────────────
     Twenty scenes are drawn from these twelve values. The faces are the zinc
     ramp so the cube sits on the product's own surfaces, and
     `--agent-cube-accent` is the single knob — the accent's top and right faces
     are mixed from it in oklab, so re-pointing this one line recolours every
     scene without touching a component. */
  --agent-cube-top: hsl(240 5% 21%);
  --agent-cube-left: hsl(240 5% 17%);
  --agent-cube-right: hsl(240 5% 14%);
  --agent-cube-stroke: hsl(240 5% 31%);
  --agent-cube-accent: var(--color-action-bright);
  /* Error is the one state that leaves the accent, because it has to: a blue
     failure looks like a blue success. These are --destructive, lit for the
     three faces the way the accent is. */
  --agent-cube-error-top: hsl(0 60% 46%);
  --agent-cube-error-left: hsl(0 62% 39%);
  --agent-cube-error-right: hsl(0 63% 33%);
  --agent-cube-error-stroke: hsl(0 68% 58%);
  /* The sixth face of the idle cube — the one plane the isometric scenes never
     show, so it has no counterpart above. */
  --agent-cube-back: hsl(240 6% 10%);
  /* Mixed into the dashed cube's stroke to grey it back from the accent. */
  --agent-cube-ghost-ink: hsl(240 5% 45%);
  /* Mixed into the accent's right face to shade it. */
  --agent-cube-accent-shade: hsl(217 40% 32%);

  /* ── Code highlighting ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
     Same eight roles as the light block, resolved through the same `-ink`
     tokens — see the note there. On dark these are the lifted ends of each
     ramp, which is what `--action-ink`/`--value-ink`/etc. already resolve to
     in this theme block. */
  --code-keyword: var(--action-ink);
  --code-string: var(--success-ink);
  --code-comment: var(--muted-foreground);
  --code-function: var(--info-ink);
  --code-number: var(--value-ink);
  --code-punctuation: var(--foreground);
  --code-type: var(--warning-ink);
  --code-variable: var(--destructive-ink);
}

@layer base {
  * {
    @apply border-border outline-ring/50;
  }
  /* Declared per theme rather than pinned, so form controls, scrollbars and
     the caret — all of which the UA paints, not us — follow the toggle. */
  html {
    @apply font-sans;
    color-scheme: light;
    /* One owner for where an anchor lands. Every sticky header in this system
       is `--height-site-header` tall, so a `#section` link cannot park a
       heading underneath it — and no component needs a `scroll-mt-*` of its
       own to say so. */
    scroll-padding-block-start: var(--scroll-offset);
    /* Already gated: the `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` block below forces
       `scroll-behavior: auto !important` on every element, so this line is off
       for anyone who asked for it to be. Travelling to an anchor is the one
       place motion carries information — it shows you the document moved
       rather than replaced itself, which is what tells you where you came
       from in a table of contents. */
    scroll-behavior: smooth;
  }
  html.dark {
    color-scheme: dark;
  }
  /* The page has a light source.
     One off-centre radial raise over `--background`, fixed to the viewport so it
     behaves like light in the room rather than like a very tall image that
     scrolls. It fades to `transparent`, which means the falloff reveals
     `--background` itself — so the vignette is the *absence* of the glow rather
     than a second dark gradient painted on top, and it can never go muddy.

     This is a foundation, not a decoration: a flat fill at zinc 950 reads as
     black paint, and the same fill under a wide, slightly lifted glow reads as
     a deep room. Every page in the product sits on it. Opaque panels — a
     sidebar, a dialog, an inset — paint over it on purpose; the atmosphere
     belongs to the page, not to the furniture.

     No animation. RULES §4 allows exactly two perpetual motions and this is
     neither; it is weather that has already settled. */
  body {
    @apply bg-background text-foreground;
    background-image: radial-gradient(
      120% 90% at 62% 34%,
      var(--page-glow) 0%,
      transparent 64%
    );
    background-attachment: fixed;
    background-repeat: no-repeat;
    -webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;
  }
  /* Focus is always visible and always the action colour — never removed. */
  :focus-visible {
    outline: 2px solid var(--ring);
    outline-offset: 2px;
  }
  /* Numerical values render tabular so columns align and live updates do not jitter. */
  .tabular {
    font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums;
  }
  /* A wash of the action colour rather than the browser's own blue. Mixed from
     the token so it follows a rebrand, and kept as a tint rather than a fill so
     the selected glyphs stay at full contrast in both themes. */
  ::selection {
    background: color-mix(in oklab, var(--color-action) 35%, transparent);
    color: var(--foreground);
  }
}

import { clsx, type ClassValue } from "clsx"
import { extendTailwindMerge } from "tailwind-merge"

// Teaches tailwind-merge our text-* scale so sizes are not mistaken for colours.
const FONT_SIZES = [
  "display",
  "h1",
  "h2",
  "h3",
  "h4",
  "lead",
  "body",
  "small",
  "nav",
  "badge",
  "code",
  "identifier",
  "number-sm",
  "number-base",
  "number-md",
  "number-lg",
  "number-xl",
] as const

// Same for shadow-*: custom elevation names must not be read as colours.
const SHADOWS = [
  "e1",
  "e2",
  "e3",
  "e4",
  "key",
  "key-down",
  "pressed",
  "btn",
  "btn-primary",
  "btn-value",
  "btn-down",
  "chip",
  "glow-action",
  "glow-value",
] as const

// Custom radius names get their own group so they merge with rounded-*.
const RADII = ["pill"] as const

export const twMerge = extendTailwindMerge({
  extend: {
    classGroups: {
      "font-size": [{ text: [...FONT_SIZES] }],
      shadow: [{ shadow: [...SHADOWS] }],
      rounded: [{ rounded: [...RADII] }],
    },
  },
})

export function cn(...inputs: ClassValue[]) {
  return twMerge(clsx(inputs))
}
